title: Linking words: and, but, or, so, because
tagline: Turning two short sentences into one — and, but, or, so, because, and more.
why: Linking words turn two short, robotic sentences into one that sounds natural — exactly what Writing Parts 6 and 7 reward. Reading Part 5 tests them directly too, choosing the right connector to complete a text. Get and/but/or/so/because right and your writing jumps up a level.

hook.text: Nadia is writing about the school trip. "We arrived, and then we had lunch. The museum was great, but the bus journey was long, so I slept!" "Nice sentences," says Miss Vega. "You joined three short ideas into one."
hook.ask: Nadia uses three small words — and, but, so — to join her ideas. Can you say what job each one does?

diagrams.title: Join two short sentences

before.text: I like football. I don't like basketball.

after.text: I like football, but I don't like basketball.

steps: Find the connection between the two ideas: same, different, reason or result?
Choose the linking word that matches.
Join the sentences and add a comma if it sounds like two parts.

diagrams.title: Where does the linking word go?

sentences.note: because + reason, after the main idea
before + action, at the start of the sentence
and… too — adding a similar idea

diagrams.caption: A linking word can join two full ideas in the middle, or start the sentence — the meaning doesn't change.

head: Linking word
Meaning
Example
rows: I play football and I play tennis.
I like football, but I don't like rugby.
Do you want tea or coffee?
It was raining, so we stayed inside.
We stayed inside because it was raining.

use.point: and, but, or — joining two ideas

examples.text: I play football and I play tennis.
I like maths, but I don't like science.
examples.note: but = a contrast, a different idea
or = a choice between two things

use.point: so and because — reason and result

examples.text: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
examples.note: so + result — comes after the reason

examples.text: We stayed inside because it was raining.
examples.note: because + reason — often comes after the result

examples.text: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
examples.note: because can also start the sentence, with a comma

examples.text: I was tired, that's why I went to bed early.
examples.note: that's why = so, a more informal result

use.point: then, after that, when, before, after, while — putting events in time

examples.text: I did my homework. Then I watched TV.
We had lunch and after that we played football.
examples.note: after that = a bit more formal than then

examples.text: When the bell rang, we went outside.
examples.note: when = one action right after another

examples.text: I listened to music while I did my homework.
examples.note: while = two actions at the same time

use.point: also, too, as well — adding extra information

examples.text: I like pizza. I also like pasta.
examples.note: also usually goes before the main verb

examples.text: Sofia plays tennis. Liam plays tennis too.
examples.note: too goes at the end of the sentence
as well = too, also at the end

watch_out.wrong: Because it was raining, so we stayed inside.
watch_out.right: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
watch_out.why: Don't use because and so together — choose one.

watch_out.wrong: I like football and but I don't like rugby.
watch_out.right: I like football, but I don't like rugby.
watch_out.why: Use only one linking word between two ideas.

watch_out.right: I also like pasta. / I like pasta too.
watch_out.why: Also and too do the same job — don't use both together.

watch_out.wrong: We stayed inside because of it was raining.
watch_out.right: We stayed inside because it was raining.
watch_out.why: Because + subject + verb; because of + a noun (because of the rain).

watch_out.wrong: I did my homework while I will watch TV.
watch_out.right: I did my homework while I watched TV.
watch_out.why: Both actions need the same past tense.

watch_out.wrong: It's raining, that's why because we stayed inside.
watch_out.right: It's raining, that's why we stayed inside.
watch_out.why: That's why already means so — don't add because as well.

l1.es: Porque llovía, nos quedamos en casa.
l1.wrong: Because it was raining, so we stayed at home.
l1.right: Because it was raining, we stayed at home.
l1.why: English only needs one linking word to show reason and result — not two.

l1.right: I also like football. / I like football too.
l1.why: Too goes at the end of the sentence; also goes before the main verb, not at the start.

l1.es: Es por eso que llegamos tarde.
l1.wrong: It's for that we arrived late.
l1.why: The fixed phrase in English is that's why, not a word-for-word translation.

l1.wrong: During I study, I listen to music.
l1.right: While I study, I listen to music.
l1.why: While + subject + verb links two actions; during needs a noun (during class).

l1.es: Me gusta el fútbol y también el tenis.
l1.wrong: I like football and also tennis, too.
l1.why: Don't stack also and too in the same sentence — choose one.

remember.trick: AND adds, BUT fights, OR picks, SO/BECAUSE explain.
remember.tip: Ask yourself: same idea (and), different idea (but), a choice (or), a reason (because) or a result (so)?

dialogue.title: Writing the class blog post
dialogue.context: Nadia, Mateo and Miss Vega write a short blog post together about the school trip to Cusco.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Let's start. What did we do first?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: We arrived, and then we had lunch.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I liked the museum, but I didn't like the bus journey.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good! Why didn't you like the bus?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Because it was very long — six hours!

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: It was tiring, so we slept on the bus.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: We visited the market, and after that we walked to the square.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I bought a hat. Sofia bought one too.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Great sentences! Do you want to write about the food or the hotel next?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: The food! It was amazing while it was also cheap.

items.sentence: I like football but I don't like rugby.
Because it was raining, so we stayed inside.
items.fix: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
items.why: don't use because and so together

items.sentence: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
I also like pasta too.

items.sentence: We stayed inside because it was raining.
We stayed inside because of it was raining.
items.fix: We stayed inside because it was raining.
items.why: because of needs a noun, not a full clause

items.sentence: I did my homework while I listened to music.
It's raining, that's why because we stayed inside.
items.fix: It's raining, that's why we stayed inside.
items.why: that's why already means so — no extra because

can_do: I can join two short sentences with and, but, or, so and because.
I can put events in order with then, after that, when, before, after and while.
I can add extra information with also, too and as well.
summary: And, but, or join two ideas: adding, contrast or a choice.
So gives the result, because gives the reason — never use them together.
Then, after that, when, before, after and while put events in time order.
Also goes before the verb; too and as well go at the end of the sentence.
Joining two short sentences with one linking word is the key to a good answer in Writing Parts 6 and 7.
